items.title: Rise of the Kakatiyas & the Line of Rulers
items.body:
### Rise of the Kakatiyas

**In one line**
The Kakatiyas (c.1163–1323) were the first dynasty to turn the Telugu-speaking land into one kingdom, ruling from Warangal (Orugallu).

**Why it is asked**
This is the foundation of AP/Telangana medieval history — every later Telugu power looked back to the Kakatiyas, so APPSC tests their origin, capital and ruler-order.

**The story (vassals who became kings)**
The Kakatiyas first served as **feudatories** (local chiefs under a greater king) — first of the **Rashtrakutas**, then of the **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** — in the dry Telangana uplands. As Chalukya power faded, **Rudradeva (also called Prataparudra I)** threw off his overlord and declared himself an independent king in **1163 CE**; we know this from the **Anumakonda (Hanamkonda) inscription**. A telling cultural shift followed: from his reign the dynasty's inscriptions began to appear in **Telugu** instead of Kannada. The capital later moved from **Hanamkonda** to the great rock-fort city of **Orugallu (Warangal)**. The family took its name from its clan goddess **Kakati** (a form of Durga), and its royal badge was the mythical bird **Garuda**.

**Picture it (rulers in order)**

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) | c.1163–1195 | Declared sovereignty; Thousand Pillar Temple |
| Mahadeva | c.1195–1199 | Short reign |
| Ganapati Deva | 1199–1262 | Greatest ruler; delta expansion; Motupalli charter |
| Rudrama Devi | c.1262–1289 | Rare woman ruler; praised by Marco Polo |
| Prataparudra II | 1289–1323 | Last ruler; fell to the Tughlaqs (1323) |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory/vassal:** a local ruler who serves and pays tribute to a stronger king.
- **Inscription:** writing carved on stone or copper — the main evidence for this era.
- **Orugallu:** the Telugu name of Warangal ('one stone'), after its single-rock fort hill.

**Don't confuse**
- **Prataparudra I** (= Rudradeva, who founded sovereignty in 1163) is a different king from **Prataparudra II** (the last ruler, fell in 1323).
- **Kakati** is the goddess the dynasty is named after; **Garuda** is its emblem bird.

**Remember it**
Ruler chain 'Ru-Ma-Ga-Ru-Pra' = **Ru**dradeva → **Ma**hadeva → **Ga**napati → **Ru**drama → **Pra**taparudra II.

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiyas ruled c.1163–1323 from Orugallu (Warangal), shifting from Hanamkonda (Anumakonda).
- They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
- Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163 (Anumakonda inscription); Telugu replaced Kannada in inscriptions.
- Ruler order: Rudradeva → Mahadeva → Ganapati Deva → Rudrama Devi → Prataparudra II.
- Royal emblem was Garuda; the family name derives from the goddess Kakati (a form of Durga).
keyPoints: Kakatiyas ruled c.1163–1323 from Orugallu (Warangal), shifting from Hanamkonda (Anumakonda).
They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163 (Anumakonda inscription); Telugu replaced Kannada in inscriptions.
Ruler order: Rudradeva → Mahadeva → Ganapati Deva → Rudrama Devi → Prataparudra II.
Royal emblem was Garuda; the family name derives from the goddess Kakati (a form of Durga).
items.mnemonic: Ruler chain 'Ru-Ma-Ga-Ru-Pra' = Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Ganapati, Rudrama, Prataparudra II.

items.title: Ganapati Deva & the Motupalli Charter
items.body:
### Ganapati Deva and the Motupalli charter

**In one line**
Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya king — he unified the Telugu lands, built the Warangal fort and the Pakhal lake, and protected traders through the Motupalli charter.

**Why it is asked**
He links three favourite exam themes in one reign: territorial unification, tank-irrigation and medieval trade policy.

**The story (unite, irrigate, trade)**
Ganapati Deva had the longest and most expansive reign of the dynasty. He pushed Kakatiya rule down from the Telangana uplands into the fertile **lowland deltas of the Godavari and Krishna rivers**, bringing most Telugu-speaking people under one crown for the first time. To defend his seat he ringed **Orugallu with a massive granite wall**, ramparts, bastions and a moat. To feed a dry land he had the huge man-made **Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake** dug — one of a chain of Kakatiya **'tanks' (reservoirs)** such as Laknavaram and Ramappa Cheruvu, many still watering fields today. Most forward-looking was his trade policy: at the port of **Motupalli** (in modern **Prakasam district**) he issued the **Abhaya Sasanam** — an 'edict of fearlessness' — promising **foreign merchants the safety of their persons and goods** and charging only a **fixed, moderate customs duty**. This drew sea-traders and made Motupalli a flourishing port.

**Picture it (three achievements)**

| Area | What he did |
|---|---|
| Territory | Extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta |
| Water | Built Pakhal Lake; chain of irrigation tanks |
| Trade | Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam protecting merchants |

**Terms explained**
- **Tank:** a man-made reservoir storing rain water for irrigation.
- **Abhaya Sasanam:** 'charter of safety/fearlessness' — a royal promise of protection to merchants.
- **Customs duty:** a tax on goods entering or leaving a port.
- **Cascade (chain) of tanks:** a series of tanks linked so that the overflow of one fills the next — the Kakatiya way of storing water in the semi-arid Telugu uplands. Pakhal, Laknavaram and the Ramappa tank (Ramappa Cheruvu) at Palampet are Kakatiya-period reservoirs.

**Culture at his court**
His elephant-general (Gajasenapati) **Jayapa Senani** wrote **Nrittaratnavali**, a Sanskrit treatise on dance (c.1253) that also describes the folk (desi) dances of the Telugu land.

**Don't confuse**
- A **brahmadeya/agrahara** grant gave tax-free land to Brahmins; the **Abhaya Sasanam** instead protected **merchants** — different kinds of charter.
- **Motupalli** was the Kakatiya port; it is not the same as the later Qutb Shahi port of Masulipatnam, though both lie on the same coast (Marco Polo's 'Mutfili' is Motupalli).

**Remember it**
Motupalli = 'Merchants Openly Trade, Under Protection' — the Abhaya (fearlessness) charter of Ganapati Deva.

**TL;DR**
- Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya; extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta.
- He walled Orugallu in granite and created the man-made Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake.
- The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam guaranteed safety and fixed low duties for overseas merchants.
- Motupalli (Prakasam district) was the chief Kakatiya port.
- Kakatiya 'tanks' (Pakhal, Laknavaram, Ramappa Cheruvu) pioneered upland reservoir irrigation.
keyPoints: Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya; extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta.
He walled Orugallu in granite and created the man-made Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake.
The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam guaranteed safety and fixed low duties for overseas merchants.
Motupalli (Prakasam district) was the chief Kakatiya port.
Kakatiya 'tanks' (Pakhal, Laknavaram, Ramappa Cheruvu) pioneered upland reservoir irrigation.
Jayapa Senani, Ganapati Deva's elephant-general, wrote the dance treatise Nrittaratnavali.
Kakatiyas built a chain (cascade) system of tanks in the semi-arid uplands — Pakhal, Laknavaram, Ramappa tank (Palampet).

items.title: Rudrama Devi & Marco Polo
items.body:
### Rudrama Devi and Marco Polo

**In one line**
Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the very few women to rule a kingdom in her own right in medieval India, and the traveller Marco Polo praised her government.

**Why it is asked**
She is a rare woman sovereign, and her link to Marco Polo gives examiners both a gender-and-governance angle and a foreign-source angle.

**The story (a queen who ruled as king)**
Ganapati Deva had no son, so he groomed his daughter **Rudrama Devi** to succeed him. She married **Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukyan prince of Nidadavolu**, but she herself held the throne. To command the loyalty of nobles unused to a woman ruler, she took a **male royal style (Rudradeva Maharaja)**. She proved a strong defender: she **beat back invasions by the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri**, and she strengthened the capital, raising her father's wall at Orugallu and adding an **outer earthen wall and a wide moat**. Having no son of her own, she named her **grandson Prataparudra II** as heir. During or just after her reign the Venetian traveller **Marco Polo** passed through (around **1289–1293**) and wrote admiringly of the justice and wealth of her kingdom, which he called **'Mutfili'** — a name taken from the port region near **Masulipatnam** — and noted its diamonds.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Reign | c.1262–1289 |
| Marriage | Virabhadra of Nidadavolu (Eastern Chalukya) |
| Defended against | Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri |
| Foreign witness | Marco Polo — kingdom 'Mutfili' |

**Terms explained**
- **Sovereign / queen regnant:** a ruler who holds power in her own right, not merely a king's consort.
- **Mutfili:** Marco Polo's name for the Kakatiya kingdom, after its port Motupalli.

**Don't confuse**
- **Rudrama Devi** (the Kakatiya queen) is not the earlier **Rudradeva** (Prataparudra I) — she only adopted a similar royal name.
- Marco Polo was **Venetian** (from Venice); do not place him with Arab travellers like Al-Biruni.

**Remember it**
'Rudrama ruled, Marco marvelled at Mutfili' — ties the queen to Marco Polo's name for her land.

**TL;DR**
- Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the few women sovereigns of medieval India.
- She married Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Nidadavolu, and took a male royal title.
- She repelled the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri and strengthened Orugallu's fortifications.
- Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) praised her rule and called the kingdom 'Mutfili' (after the port of Motupalli).
- Lacking a son, she nominated her grandson Prataparudra II as successor.
keyPoints: Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the few women sovereigns of medieval India.
She married Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Nidadavolu.

Lacking a son, she nominated her grandson Prataparudra II as successor.

items.title: Prataparudra II & the Fall of Warangal
items.body:
### Prataparudra II and the fall of Warangal

**In one line**
Prataparudra II was the last Kakatiya king; after resisting three Delhi Sultanate sieges, Warangal fell in 1323 and the dynasty ended.

**Why it is asked**
The fall of the Kakatiyas is a turning point — it brought the Delhi Sultanate into the Deccan and set off the Telugu resistance that followed.

**The story (three sieges and the end)**
**Prataparudra II** (r. **1289–1323**) spent his reign fighting off **Delhi Sultanate** armies. An early Khalji raid was beaten back at the **Battle of Upparapalli (1303)**. But in **1310** Alauddin Khalji's general **Malik Kafur** besieged Orugallu and forced Prataparudra to pay a yearly **tribute**; tradition says the famous **Koh-i-Noor diamond** went to Delhi at this time. A further siege in **1318** squeezed renewed submission out of him. The end came in **1323**, when **Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan)** — son of Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** — captured Warangal after a long siege. Prataparudra was taken prisoner and is believed to have **died near the river Narmada** while being marched to Delhi. The victors renamed Orugallu **Sultanpur**, and the leaderless Telugu country sank into confusion under Delhi's governors.

**Picture it (the sieges)**

| Year | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1303 | Khalji raid defeated at Upparapalli |
| 1310 | Malik Kafur forces tribute; Koh-i-Noor said to go to Delhi |
| 1318 | Fresh siege; renewed submission |
| 1323 | Ulugh Khan conquers Warangal; dynasty ends |

**Terms explained**
- **Tribute:** regular payment made by a weaker ruler to a stronger one to avoid attack.
- **Ulugh Khan:** the title of prince Jauna Khan, who later ruled as Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
- **Nayankara system:** the Kakatiya arrangement of warrior chiefs (nayakas) who held land in return for military obligations. The nayaka rank was open to men of any birth — peasants recruited into the army could rise into it — so it fostered social mobility. It was most fully organised under Prataparudra II.

**Don't confuse**
- **1310 (Malik Kafur, Khalji)** only forced tribute; **1323 (Ulugh Khan, Tughlaq)** actually ended the dynasty.
- **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** was the Sultan who ordered the 1323 campaign; **Ulugh Khan** was the field commander who led it.

**Remember it**
Three sieges '10-18-23' (1310, 1318, 1323) — the third one ended the dynasty and renamed Warangal 'Sultanpur'.

**TL;DR**
- Prataparudra II (1289–1323) was the last Kakatiya ruler.
- 1310: Malik Kafur's siege forced tribute; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have gone to Delhi.
- 1323: Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan), sent by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, finally conquered Warangal.
- Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur after 1323.
- Prataparudra reportedly died near the Narmada while being taken prisoner to Delhi.
keyPoints: Prataparudra II (1289–1323) was the last Kakatiya ruler.
1310: Malik Kafur's siege forced tribute; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have gone to Delhi.
1323: Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan), sent by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, finally conquered Warangal.
Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur after 1323.
Prataparudra reportedly died near the Narmada while being taken prisoner to Delhi.
items.mnemonic: Three sieges '10-18-23' (1310, 1318, 1323) — the third one ended the dynasty.

items.title: Kakatiya Art, Ramappa Temple & UNESCO 2021
items.body:
### Kakatiya art and the Ramappa Temple

**In one line**
The Kakatiyas built a distinctive temple style whose finest surviving example, the Ramappa Temple, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

**Why it is asked**
Art-and-architecture questions are reliable scorers, and Ramappa is a flagship AP/Telangana heritage fact with a precise year (2021) examiners love.

**The story (stone, bricks and a sculptor's name)**
Kakatiya builders developed clear trademarks: temples raised on **star-shaped platforms**, door-jambs and pillars of **polished black dolerite**, and towers (**vimanas**) built from specially **light 'floating bricks'**. Their landmark monuments are the **Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda** (built by Rudradeva, 1163), the great **Warangal Fort** with its ornamental **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (the Kirti Torana gateways, now the **emblem of Telangana**), and above all the **Ramappa Temple**. Ramappa stands at **Palampet (Mulugu district)**, built in **1213** by **Recherla Rudra**, a general of **Ganapati Deva**, and dedicated to Shiva as **Rudreshwara**. Unusually, the temple is popularly named not after the god or the king but after its **sculptor, Ramappa**. Its engineering still amazes: a **floating-brick** tower that reduces weight, and a **sand-box foundation** that cushions earthquakes, while its dolerite figures keep a **mirror polish after 800 years**. UNESCO inscribed it in **2021** (44th session) as the **'Kakatiya Rudreswara (Ramappa) Temple'** (List No. 1570).

**Picture it**

| Monument | Builder / note |
|---|---|
| Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanamkonda | Rudradeva, 1163 |
| Warangal Fort & Kala Thoranam | Kakatiya; gateways = Telangana emblem |
| Ramappa Temple, Palampet | Recherla Rudra, 1213; UNESCO 2021 |

**Terms explained**
- **Vimana:** the tower built over a temple's main shrine in the South Indian style.
- **Floating bricks:** bricks made so porous and light that they can float in water, used to lighten the tower.
- **Sand-box foundation:** a pit filled with sand under the temple that absorbs earthquake shocks.
- **Dolerite:** a very hard dark stone the Kakatiyas polished to a mirror shine.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramappa Temple (Kakatiya, UNESCO 2021)** is a built-up stone temple — not a rock-cut monolith like the Mahabalipuram rathas.
- The **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (gateway) is the Telangana emblem; do not confuse it with the Qutb Shahi **Charminar**.

**Remember it**
Ramappa = 'the temple named after its artist' + **UNESCO 2021**; look for 'floating bricks' and 'sand-box foundation'.

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiya style: floating bricks for towers, polished dolerite carvings, star-shaped platforms.
- Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple, Palampet — built 1213 by Recherla Rudra, general of Ganapati Deva.
- It is uniquely named after its sculptor Ramappa; famed for its sand-box (earthquake-resistant) foundation.
- Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 (44th session), List No. 1570; UNESCO officially lists it as the 'Kakatiya Rudreswara (Ramappa) Temple'.
- Other monuments: Thousand Pillar Temple (Hanamkonda), Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam (Telangana emblem).

items.title: Musunuri Nayakas & the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
items.body:
### Musunuri Nayakas and the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi

**In one line**
After the Kakatiyas fell, the Musunuri Nayakas led a Telugu revolt that recovered Warangal from Delhi in 1336; the earlier Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi had already given Telugu its first great literature.

**Why it is asked**
The Musunuri recovery is the bridge between the Kakatiyas and the Reddi/Vijayanagara era, and the Eastern Chalukyas explain where written Telugu literature began.

**The story (resistance after the fall)**
When Warangal fell in 1323, the Telugu country was left under Delhi's governors and sank into disorder. Out of this rose the **Musunuri Nayakas**, who claimed to carry on the **Kakatiya legacy**. **Prolaya Nayaka**, ruling from **Rekapalle near Bhadrachalam** (around 1330), issued the **Vilasa copper-plate grant** that mourns the ruin of the Telugu land and presents him as the restorer of order; he died without children. His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (r. 1333–1368)** then built a wider alliance and, aided (per the Kaluvacheru grant) by **75 Nayakas** and the Hoysala king **Veera Ballala III**, **recovered Warangal from the Tughlaq governor Malik Maqbul in 1336**. Kapaya took the proud title **'Andhra Suratrana'** ('Sultan of the Andhra country'). But he steadily lost ground — including **Golconda** — to the rising **Bahmani Sultanate**, and was finally defeated and killed by rival **Recherla Nayakas at Bhimavaram in 1368**.

**A step back — the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi**
Long before, the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (coastal Andhra) were founded by **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** around **624 CE**. Their king **Rajaraja Narendra** patronised the poet **Nannaya**, the 'Adi Kavi' (first poet), who began the **Telugu Mahabharatamu**. A Chalukya–Chola royal marriage later produced **Kulottunga I**, who took the imperial Chola throne, merging the two lines.

**Terms explained**
- **Nayaka:** a warrior-chief holding land in return for military service.
- **Copper-plate grant:** a royal order engraved on copper sheets — a key historical source.
- **Adi Kavi:** 'the first poet' — the title given to Nannaya in Telugu literature.

**Don't confuse**
- **Prolaya Nayaka** issued the Vilasa grant (c.1330); **Kapaya Nayaka** recovered Warangal (1336). Keep the two cousins apart.
- The **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (coastal Andhra, 7th c. onward) are different from the **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** the Kakatiyas served.

**Remember it**
Musunuri pair: 'Prolaya **writes** (Vilasa 1330), Kapaya **wins** (Warangal 1336)'. Telugu literature starts with **Nannaya** under the Eastern Chalukyas.

**TL;DR**
- Musunuri Nayakas led Telugu resistance after the collapse of the Kakatiyas, claiming to continue the Kakatiya legacy.
- Prolaya Nayaka (Rekapalle, near Bhadrachalam) issued the Vilasa grant c.1330.
- Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal from Malik Maqbul in 1336 with 75 Nayakas and Hoysala help.
- Kapaya took the title 'Andhra Suratrana' and was killed by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368.
- Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi: founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana (c.624); Rajaraja Narendra patronised Nannaya; the Chola union produced Kulottunga I.

items.title: Kakatiya Origins, Early Chiefs & Rudradeva (Prataparudra I)
items.body:
### Kakatiya Origins, Early Chiefs & Rudradeva (Prataparudra I)

**In one line**
Before 1163 the Kakatiyas were a line of Chalukya vassals at Anumakonda; Rudradeva turned them into a sovereign Telugu dynasty, wrote on statecraft and built the Thousand Pillar Temple.

**The story**
The earliest chief we know is **Beta I**. **Prola I** received **Anumakonda** (Hanamkonda) as a fief from the Western Chalukya king **Someshvara I**, and **Prola II** made the family powerful while still a vassal (the source PDF calls him the founder). His son **Rudradeva**, also called **Prataparudra I**, declared independence in **1163**, defeated the **Velanati Chodas**, wrote the **Nitisara**, and built the **Thousand Pillar Temple**. In his time the **Palnadu war** was fought at **Karempudi**. His brother **Mahadeva** was killed by the Yadavas, and the young **Ganapati** was held captive by the Yadava **Jaitugi** before he came home to rule.

#### Early chiefs

| Chief | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Beta I** | c.1000–1052 | Earliest known chief; a feudatory in the Hanamkonda area |
| **Prola I** | c.1052–1076 | Received **Anumakonda** as a fief from the Western Chalukya **Someshvara I** |
| **Prola II** | c.1116–1157 | Named founder in the PDF; built up Kakatiya power while still a Chalukya vassal; died fighting the Velanati Chodas |
| **Mahadeva** | c.1195–1199 | Killed fighting the Yadavas; son Ganapati was held captive by the Yadava **Jaitugi**, then released |
| **Clan & name** | — | Claimed **Durjaya** lineage; name from the goddess Kakati or the place Kakatipura |

#### Rudradeva (Prataparudra I, c.1158–1195)

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Nitisara** | Sanskrit work on statecraft by Prataparudra I (Rudradeva) |
| **Thousand Pillar Temple** | Hanamkonda, **1163**; a star-shaped trikuta for Shiva (Rudreshwara), Vishnu and **Surya**; monolithic Nandi |
| **Palnadu war** | Battle of **Karempudi** (c.1182) — a civil war of Haihaya chiefs (Brahmanaidu, Nayakuralu); sung in the Palnati Viracharitra |
| **Velanati Chodas** | Rudradeva defeated them, pushing towards the coast |
| **Language shift** | Inscriptions moved from **Kannada** to **Telugu** — a marker of Telugu political identity |

**Don't confuse**
- **Prola II** built the power; **Rudradeva** declared sovereignty (1163). Exams also call Rudradeva the founder of the independent kingdom.
- The **Palnadu war** was a war among local Haihaya chiefs, not a Kakatiya–Delhi war.
- **Thousand Pillar Temple** (Hanamkonda, 1163) ≠ **Ramappa temple** (Palampet, 1213).

**TL;DR**
- Beta I → Prola I (Anumakonda fief) → Beta II → Prola II → Rudradeva (1163).
- Rudradeva: Nitisara; Thousand Pillar trikuta (Shiva, Vishnu, Surya).
- Palnadu war — Karempudi (c.1182).
- Mahadeva killed by the Yadavas; Ganapati held by Jaitugi.
keyPoints: Prola I received Anumakonda as a fief from the Western Chalukya Someshvara I.
Prola II built up Kakatiya power; Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163.
Rudradeva wrote the Nitisara and built the Thousand Pillar Temple — a trikuta of Shiva, Vishnu and Surya.
The Palnadu war (Battle of Karempudi, c.1182) took place in his reign.
Kakatiya inscriptions shifted from Kannada to Telugu.

items.title: Ganapati Deva & Rudrama Devi — Court, Family and Sources
items.body:
### Ganapati Deva & Rudrama Devi — Court, Family and Sources

**In one line**
Beyond the Pakhal lake and the Motupalli charter, exams ask who wrote under Ganapati Deva, how Rudrama ruled as a "king", who rebelled against her, and which inscription records her death.

**The story**
Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) welcomed the poet **Tikkana**, who completed 15 parvas of the Telugu Mahabharata and persuaded him to restore **Manuma Siddhi** to Nellore. Ganapati's sister **Mailamba** left the **Bayyaram tank inscription**, our best Kakatiya family tree. Late in life he lost to the Pandya **Jatavarman Sundara Pandya** at **Muttukuru**. With no son, he made his elder daughter **Rudrama** heir. She ruled as **Rudradeva Maharaja**, faced the revolt of the Kayastha chief **Ambadeva**, and died in **1289** (the **Chandupatla inscription**). The first Telugu Ramayana, by **Gona Budda Reddy**, belongs to her age. The **Venetian** traveller **Marco Polo** came soon after and called the land **Mutfili**, after the port **Motupalli**.

#### Ganapati Deva — court and family

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Tikkana Somayaji** | Translated **15 parvas** of the Mahabharata into Telugu; also wrote Nirvachanottara Ramayanamu; honoured by Ganapati Deva |
| **Manuma Siddhi** | Ganapati restored this Telugu Choda ruler to **Nellore** at Tikkana's request |
| **Ganapamba** | His second daughter (married to Kota Beta); Rudrama, the elder, was groomed to rule |
| **Bayyaram tank inscription** | Set up by **Mailamba**, Ganapati's sister — the main source for the early Kakatiya family tree |
| **Muttukuru** (c.1263) | The Pandya **Jatavarman Sundara Pandya** defeated the ageing Ganapati near Nellore |

#### Rudrama Devi — rule and sources

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Male title** | Ruled as **Rudradeva Maharaja** to win the loyalty of nobles |
| **Kayastha rebellion** | The Kayastha chief **Ambadeva** rebelled and allied with her enemies |
| **Chandupatla inscription** | In Nalgonda district — records her death in **1289**, probably fighting Ambadeva |
| **Ranganatha Ramayanam** | First Telugu Ramayana (dvipada metre) by **Gona Budda** Reddy, a feudatory |
| **Heir** | Her grandson **Prataparudra II**, son of her daughter **Mummadamma** |
| **Marco Polo** | **Venetian**; on his way home from China he visited the Kakatiya coast (c.**1292**–93) and praised the queen's justice |
| **Mutfili** | Marco Polo's name for the kingdom, from the port of **Motupalli**; he noted its diamonds and fine cotton |

**Don't confuse**
- **Rudradeva** (Prataparudra I, a man, 1163) ≠ **Rudradeva Maharaja** (the title of Queen Rudrama).
- **Mutfili** = Motupalli (Kakatiya port); **Maabar** = Marco Polo's name for the Pandya coast.
- **Ranganatha Ramayanam** (Gona Budda Reddy) is Telugu; **Kamba Ramayanam** is Tamil.

**TL;DR**
- Tikkana (15 parvas) was honoured by Ganapati Deva; Manuma Siddhi restored to Nellore.
- Bayyaram tank inscription of Mailamba — Kakatiya genealogy.
- Rudrama ruled as 'Rudradeva Maharaja'; Ambadeva's revolt; Chandupatla inscription — death 1289.
- Marco Polo (Venetian): 'Mutfili' = Motupalli.
keyPoints: Tikkana Somayaji translated 15 parvas of the Mahabharata into Telugu in the age of Ganapati Deva.
The Bayyaram tank inscription of Mailamba, sister of Ganapati Deva, gives the Kakatiya genealogy.
Rudrama Devi ruled as 'Rudradeva Maharaja'; the Kayastha chief Ambadeva rebelled; the Chandupatla inscription records her death in 1289.
Gona Budda Reddy wrote the Ranganatha Ramayanam, the first Telugu Ramayana.
Marco Polo, a Venetian, called the kingdom 'Mutfili' after the port of Motupalli.

items.title: Prataparudra II — Sieges in Detail, Nayankara and Village Administration
items.body:
### Prataparudra II — Sieges in Detail, Nayankara and Village Administration

**In one line**
The fall of Warangal took twenty years and five Delhi expeditions; the Kakatiya state that resisted them rested on nayakas holding land for military service and on self-run villages.

**The story**
**Prataparudra II** (1289–1323) beat a Khalji army at **Upparapalli** (1303), but paid tribute to **Malik Kafur** (1310) and to **Khusrau Khan** (1318). **Ulugh Khan**'s first siege (1321) collapsed, and his second (1323), ordered by **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, ended the dynasty. A converted Kakatiya officer, **Malik Maqbul**, then governed for Delhi and later rose to be Firoz Tughlaq's **wazir**. The kingdom rested on the **Nayankara** system: a nayaka held land (**nayankaramu**) for keeping troops, and Prataparudra put each of Warangal's **77 bastions** under one. In the villages a body of twelve **Ayagars** — the Reddi, Karanam, Talari and others — ran local affairs. At court **Vidyanatha** wrote the **Prataparudriyam**.

#### The five Delhi expeditions

| Year | What happened |
|---|---|
| **1303** | Khalji army defeated at **Upparapalli** |
| **1310** | **Malik Kafur** besieged Warangal; Prataparudra paid tribute (Koh-i-Noor said to go to Delhi) |
| **1318** | **Khusrau Khan** (under Mubarak Shah Khalji) besieged Warangal again and exacted tribute |
| **1321** | Ulugh Khan's first siege failed (rumours in his camp); he returned in 1323 |
| **1323** | Sultan **Ghiyasuddin** Tughlaq sent his son **Ulugh Khan** (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq); Warangal fell; renamed Sultanpur |
| **Malik Maqbul** | A converted Kakatiya commander (Gannama Nayaka); Delhi's governor at Warangal; later Firoz Tughlaq's **wazir** (Khan-i-Jahan) |

#### Administration and court

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **77 bastions** | Prataparudra II placed each of the **77 bastions** of Warangal under a nayaka — the Nayankara at its height |
| **Padmanayakas** | Velama warrior chiefs in Kakatiya service (the later Recherla Nayakas were Padmanayakas) |
| **Angarakshas** | The king's personal bodyguards |
| **Ayagars** | Twelve hereditary village servants — the **Reddi** (headman), **Karanam** (accountant), Talari (watchman) and others |
| **Nayankaramu** | Land assigned to a nayaka in return for keeping **troops** for the king — later adopted by Vijayanagara |
| **Prataparudriyam** | Sanskrit poetics by **Vidyanatha**, illustrated with verses praising Prataparudra II |

**Don't confuse**
- **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** ordered the 1323 campaign; **Ulugh Khan** (his son, later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) led it.
- **Nayankara** (land for military service) ≠ **Ayagar** system (village servants).
- **Malik Kafur** (1310) only took tribute; the kingdom ended in 1323.

**TL;DR**
- 1303 Upparapalli victory; 1310 Malik Kafur; 1318 Khusrau Khan; 1321 failed siege; 1323 fall.
- Malik Maqbul: converted Kakatiya officer, later wazir of Firoz Tughlaq.
- Nayankaramu = land for keeping troops; 77 bastions under nayakas; Ayagars run villages.
- Vidyanatha — Prataparudriyam.
keyPoints: A Khalji army was defeated at Upparapalli (1303); Malik Kafur forced tribute in 1310; Khusrau Khan besieged Warangal in 1318.
Ulugh Khan's first siege (1321) failed; the 1323 conquest was ordered by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.
Malik Maqbul, a converted Kakatiya commander, later became Firoz Tughlaq's wazir.
Nayankara: a nayaka held land (nayankaramu) for keeping troops; Warangal had 77 bastions under nayakas; Angarakshas were royal bodyguards.
Ayagars — twelve village servants such as the Reddi (headman) and Karanam (accountant); Vidyanatha wrote the Prataparudriyam.

items.title: Kakatiya Monuments, Economy and Telugu Literature — the Details
items.body:
### Kakatiya Monuments, Economy and Telugu Literature — the Details

**In one line**
The Kakatiya age gave Telangana its fort, its gateways and its tank network, and gave Telugu its second great Mahabharata poet, its first grammar in Telugu and its Virashaiva classics.

**The story**
Ramappa became **India's 39th World Heritage Site** in 2021, at the same session that listed **Dholavira** as the 40th. It stands at **Palampet** in **Mulugu** district, and its pillars carry **madanika** dancer brackets. **Warangal Fort** had **three** walls, and the **Swayambhu** temple inside had **four** carved gateways, the **Kirti Toranas**. The tanks, such as **Ganapasamudram** at Ghanpur, inspired Telangana's **Mission Kakatiya**. Marco Polo wrote of **diamond** mines near **Kollur**. In literature, **Tikkana** joined Nannaya and later **Errana** in the **Kavitraya**, **Palkuriki Somanatha** wrote the **Basava Puranam**, and **Ketana** wrote the first Telugu grammar in Telugu.

#### Monuments

| Monument / feature | Fact |
|---|---|
| **India's 39th WHS** | Ramappa = **39th**; **Dholavira** (Harappan, Gujarat) = 40th — both at the 2021 session (held online, chaired from Fuzhou, China) |
| **Location** | **Palampet**, Venkatapur mandal, **Mulugu** district, Telangana (earlier Warangal district) |
| **Madanikas** | Bracket figures of dancers (and the Nagini) on Ramappa's outer pillars, in polished black basalt/dolerite |
| **Warangal Fort** | **Three** concentric walls — inner stone (Ganapati), middle **earthen** (Rudrama) and an outer ring, with a moat |
| **Kirti Toranas** | **Four** carved gateways of the **Swayambhu** Shiva temple in Warangal Fort — the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam |
| **Kota Gullu** | A walled Kakatiya temple group at **Ghanpur** (Mulugu district), of Ganapati Deva's time |

#### Tanks, coins and trade goods

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Ganapasamudram** | Kakatiya tank at Ghanpur (named after Ganapati Deva) |
| **Mission Kakatiya** | Telangana programme (from 2015) to restore village tanks, named after the Kakatiya cascade system |
| **Coins** | Gold **gadyana**s and smaller madas |
| **Diamonds** | Marco Polo described **diamond** mines of the Krishna valley (**Kollur** area) — source of the Koh-i-Noor |

#### Literature and religion

| Author / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Palkuriki Somanatha** | **Basava Puranam** and Panditaradhya Charitra (Telugu, Virashaiva, dvipada metre) |
| **Tikkana** | **Nirvachanottara** Ramayanamu (prose-free Ramayana); 15 parvas of the Andhra Mahabharatam |
| **Jayapa Senani** | Nritta Ratnavali (dance), **Gita Ratnavali** (song) and **Vadya Ratnavali** (instruments); elephant-general of Ganapati |
| **Ketana** | **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanamu** — first Telugu grammar in Telugu; also Dasakumaracharitramu (a pupil of Tikkana) |
| **Marana** | Telugu **Markandeya** Puranam (dedicated to a general of Prataparudra II) |
| **Baddena** | **Sumati** Satakam (moral verses; attribution traditional) and Nitisastra Muktavali |
| **Kavitraya** | Nannaya (Eastern Chalukya), Tikkana (Kakatiya age) and **Errana** (Reddi age) together completed the Telugu Mahabharata |
| **Religion** | Mainly **Shaiva** (Kalamukha and Virashaiva influence); tolerant of **Jainism** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramappa** = 39th Indian World Heritage Site (Telangana, 2021); **Dholavira** = 40th (Gujarat, 2021).
- **Basava Puranam** (Palkuriki Somanatha, Telugu) ≠ the Kannada vachanas of Basava himself.
- **Kavitraya**: Nannaya (11th c.), Tikkana (13th c.), Errana (14th c.).

**TL;DR**
- Ramappa: India's 39th WHS (2021); Dholavira the 40th; Palampet, Mulugu.
- Warangal Fort: three walls; four Kirti Toranas of the Swayambhu temple.
- Mission Kakatiya (Telangana, 2015) honours the tank system.
- Kavitraya: Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana; Palkuriki — Basava Puranam; Ketana — first Telugu grammar in Telugu.
keyPoints: Ramappa became India's 39th World Heritage Site (2021); Dholavira, at the same session, became the 40th.
Ramappa is at Palampet, Mulugu district (Telangana); madanika bracket figures adorn its pillars.
Warangal Fort had three concentric walls; the Swayambhu temple had four Kirti Toranas (Kakatiya Kala Thoranam).
Telangana's 'Mission Kakatiya' (2015) restores tanks; Kakatiya gold coins were gadyanas.
Palkuriki Somanatha — Basava Puranam; Ketana — Andhra Bhasha Bhushanamu; Kavitraya = Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana.

items.title: Musunuri Nayakas & Eastern Chalukyas — Grants, Thrones and Poets
items.body:
### Musunuri Nayakas & Eastern Chalukyas — Grants, Thrones and Poets

**In one line**
Two follow-up stories: how the Musunuri Nayakas won Warangal back and then lost it to the Bahmanis and the Recherlas, and how the Eastern Chalukya court began the Telugu Mahabharata.

**The story**
**Prolaya Nayaka** ruled from **Rekapalle** and issued the Vilasa grant. His cousin **Kapaya** recovered Warangal in 1336 — the **Kaluvacheru grant** credits **75 Nayakas** — but under Bahmani pressure he ceded **Golconda** and the **Turquoise Throne**, and in **1368** the Recherla Nayakas killed him at **Bhimavaram**. Two centuries earlier, at **Rajamahendravaram**, the Eastern Chalukya **Rajaraja Narendra** had **Nannaya** (the **Adi Kavi**) begin the Telugu Mahabharata; Tikkana carried it on and **Errana** finished the **Aranya** parva.

#### Musunuri Nayakas and the Telugu Mahabharata

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Prolaya Nayaka** | Ruled from **Rekapalle** near Bhadrachalam; Vilasa grant (c.1330) |
| **Kaluvacheru grant** | Issued by Anitalli; says Kapaya was helped by **75 Nayakas** |
| **Loss to the Bahmanis** | Kapaya ceded **Golconda** and gave the **Turquoise Throne** (Takht-i-Firoza) to Bahmani Muhammad Shah I |
| **End (1368)** | Kapaya killed by the Recherla (Velama) Nayakas at **Bhimavaram** in **1368** |
| **Errana** | Completed the **Aranya** parva left unfinished by Nannaya (Reddi age) |
| **Nannaya** | **Adi Kavi** of Telugu; wrote the first **two-and-a-half** parvas under Rajaraja Narendra; also the Sanskrit grammar Andhra Shabda Chintamani |
| **Rajaraja Narendra** | Ruled from **Rajamahendravaram** (Rajahmundry), c.1019–1061 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Turquoise Throne** (Takht-i-Firoza) went to the **Bahmanis**; the **Peacock Throne** belongs to Shah Jahan.
- **Rajaraja Narendra** (Eastern Chalukya, Rajamahendravaram) ≠ **Rajaraja I** (Chola, Thanjavur).

**TL;DR**
- Prolaya — Rekapalle; Kapaya — 75 Nayakas (Kaluvacheru grant), lost Golconda and the Turquoise Throne, killed 1368 at Bhimavaram.
- Nannaya (Adi Kavi) — 2½ parvas, Rajamahendravaram; Errana finished the Aranya parva.
keyPoints: Prolaya Nayaka ruled from Rekapalle near Bhadrachalam.
The Kaluvacheru grant says 75 Nayakas helped Kapaya Nayaka.
Kapaya Nayaka ceded Golconda and the Turquoise Throne to the Bahmani Muhammad Shah I; killed at Bhimavaram (1368).
Nannaya, the Adi Kavi, wrote two-and-a-half parvas under Rajaraja Narendra at Rajamahendravaram.

items.title: Kakatiya Reign Dates, Vengi Detail and the Aftermath of 1323
items.body:
### Kakatiya Reign Dates, Vengi Detail and the Aftermath of 1323

**In one line**
A last set of facts: the reign dates exams match against rulers, a few more Eastern Chalukya landmarks (Pishtapura, Addanki, Draksharama), and who took over the Kakatiya legacy.

**The story**
Kakatiya sovereignty ran from **1163** to **1323** under five rulers, with Ganapati Deva's 63 years the **longest** reign. The Eastern Chalukyas, a few centuries earlier, began at **Pishtapura** (Pithapuram); **Gunaga Vijayaditya III** fought the Rashtrakutas, his general **Pandaranga** left the **Addanki** inscription — the first Telugu verse inscription — and **Chalukya Bhima I** is linked with the **Draksharama** and Samalkot temples. Vengi was a **bone of contention** between the Cholas and Kalyani until it **merged** into the **Chola empire** under Kulottunga I. After 1323 the legacy passed to the Musunuri and **Recherla** Nayakas, to the Bahmanis (whom Kapaya helped through **Hasan Gangu**), and, by one tradition, to **Harihara and Bukka**, founders of Vijayanagara.

#### Reign dates

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Rudradeva** (Prataparudra I) | c.**1158–1195** | Sovereign from 1163 |
| **Mahadeva** | c.**1195–1199** | Short reign; killed by the Yadavas |
| **Ganapati Deva** | **1199–1262** | The **longest** reign (63 years); the PDF gives 1198–1262 |
| **Rudrama Devi** | c.**1262–1289** | The PDF gives 1262–1296; the Chandupatla inscription fixes her death in 1289 |
| **Prataparudra II** | **1289–1323** | Last ruler (the PDF gives 1296–1323) |

#### Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi — more landmarks

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Pishtapura** (Pithapuram) | First seat of Kubja Vishnuvardhana; Vengi became the capital later |
| **Gunaga Vijayaditya III** | 848–892; the greatest Eastern Chalukya warrior — fought the Rashtrakutas and Gangas |
| **Addanki inscription** | Of **Pandaranga**, general of Gunaga Vijayaditya III — the earliest Telugu verse (tarujoja metre) inscription (Bapatla/Prakasam coast) |
| **Chalukya Bhima I** | Bhimeswara temples at **Draksharama** and Samalkot — two of the five **Pancharama** shrines |
| **End of the Vengi line** | Vengi **merged** into the **Chola empire** when Kulottunga I took the Chola throne (1070) |
| **Vengi wars** | Vengi was a **bone of contention** between the Cholas and the Kalyani Chalukyas |

#### After 1323 — successors and later court figures

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Harihara & Bukka** | One tradition: they are said to have served Prataparudra II as treasury officers, then Kampili, before founding Vijayanagara (1336) |
| **Kapaya & the Bahmanis** | Kapaya helped **Hasan Gangu** in the 1347 revolt, but the new Bahmani state soon turned on him |
| **Recherla Nayakas** | Velama chiefs who ruled from **Rachakonda** and **Devarakonda** after killing Kapaya (1368) |
| **Recherla Prasaditya** | Rudrama's general who secured her throne — called **Kakatiya-rajya-sthapanacharya** |
| **Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya** | Virashaiva teacher; **Shivatattvasaram** (Telugu); hero of Palkuriki's Panditaradhya Charitra |
| **Extent** | Telangana, Andhra, parts of eastern Karnataka and southern **Odisha** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Addanki** (Pandaranga) = earliest Telugu **verse** inscription; **Kalamalla** (Renati Cholas, c.575) = earliest Telugu inscription.
- The PDF's reigns (Rudrama 1262–1296, Prataparudra II 1296–1323) differ from the inscriptions (1289 death of Rudrama); use 1262–1289 and 1289–1323.

**TL;DR**
- Rudradeva c.1158–1195; Mahadeva 1195–1199; Ganapati 1199–1262 (longest); Rudrama c.1262–1289; Prataparudra II 1289–1323.
- Vengi: Pishtapura first seat; Gunaga Vijayaditya III; Addanki verse inscription; Draksharama (Pancharama); merged into the Chola empire.
- Successors: Musunuri, Recherla (Rachakonda, Devarakonda), Bahmanis; tradition links Harihara and Bukka to Prataparudra II.
keyPoints: Reigns: Rudradeva c.1158–1195; Ganapati Deva 1199–1262 (longest); Rudrama Devi c.1262–1289; Prataparudra II 1289–1323.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana first ruled from Pishtapura (Pithapuram).
The Addanki inscription of Pandaranga is the earliest Telugu verse inscription.
Chalukya Bhima I is linked with the Draksharama and Samalkot Pancharama temples; Vengi merged into the Chola empire under Kulottunga I.
After 1368 the Recherla Nayakas ruled from Rachakonda and Devarakonda.

items.title: For Mains — Kakatiyas of Warangal
items.body:
### For Mains — Kakatiyas of Warangal

Mains clauses **M2-2b** and **M2-7** (paper **mains-2**) place the Kakatiyas inside 'AP medieval 1000–1565' and the Deccan dynasties. Argue them as *state-builders of the Telugu identity*, not as a date list.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Political unification | First to join upland Telangana and the coastal delta into one Telugu polity |
| Society | Nayankara system — warrior status open to any birth, giving social mobility |
| Economy | Cascade tank irrigation (Pakhal, Laknavaram) + Motupalli maritime trade |
| Culture | Telugu replaces Kannada in inscriptions; Ramappa, Thousand Pillar Temple, Kala Thoranam |
| Significance/legacy | Model for Reddi kingdoms and Vijayanagara; Telangana state emblem |
| Limitation | Dependence on feudatory nayakas; could not withstand Delhi's cavalry armies |

**Evidence to quote**
- Anumakonda inscription (1163) — the sovereignty marker; Telugu-language shift.
- Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam — a rare medieval merchant-protection charter.
- Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) on Rudrama Devi — foreign testimony on a woman ruler.
- Vilasa grant of Prolaya Nayaka (c.1330) — contemporary voice on the post-1323 devastation.
- Ramappa Temple, UNESCO World Heritage 2021 (List No. 1570) — living heritage argument.
- Cynthia Talbot and Richard Eaton — modern scholarship on Kakatiya social mobility.

**AP angle (natural, not forced)**
The Kakatiya **Kala Thoranam** is the official emblem of Telangana, and the dynasty's tanks still irrigate Telangana farms — a direct line from medieval statecraft to present-day AP/Telangana identity and water management.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: the Nayankara system as early 'social mobility' to enrich a society-and-polity answer.
- Quote: Marco Polo's praise of Rudrama Devi for a gender-and-governance point.
- Diagram idea: a Telangana map marking Warangal (Orugallu), Hanamkonda, Palampet (Ramappa), Pakhal Lake and Motupalli port.
keyPoints: Mains M2-2b/M2-7 (mains-2): frame the Kakatiyas as builders of Telugu political and cultural identity.
Strongest arguments: political unification + the Nayankara system's social mobility.
Economy line: cascade tank irrigation plus Motupalli trade via the Abhaya Sasanam.
Culture line: Telugu inscriptions, Ramappa (UNESCO 2021), Kala Thoranam (Telangana emblem).
Quote Marco Polo on Rudrama Devi and the Vilasa grant on the post-1323 devastation.
Limitation: reliance on feudatory nayakas; fell to Delhi's cavalry in 1323.
items.source: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice; Richard Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan; whc.unesco.org/en/list/1570
